title: You are right too
hookLine: as judge he tells both quarreling men they're right, and when his wife objects, tells her she's right too (Nasruddin tale)

lines: TWO MEN, RED IN THE FACE.
cards: Two friends, a couple, two coworkers, a family group chat. An argument breaks out, and both sides turn to whoever is watching: tell them I'm right. Be the judge.
Somebody has to win. In the old stories, Nasruddin gets this job for real. For a while, the tales say, he serves as the town's judge, the qadi.
Two men walk into his courtroom, red in the face, each sure the other has wronged him. Nasruddin settles into his seat and listens. What he says next is the whole joke.

teach.b: The first man tells his side. It's convincing. Nasruddin nods: you're right.
The second man jumps in, furious, and tells his side. It's convincing too. Nasruddin nods: you're right.
Then his wife, listening from the next room, and in some tellings it's a clerk or a neighbor, can't stand it. They can't both be right! Nasruddin thinks it over and says: you know, you're right too.
It's a joke first. Let it be a joke. But look at what it catches.
We tend to hear an argument as a contest with one winner, and we pick our winner fast, often before the second person has finished talking. Nasruddin can't.
Each time someone speaks, he actually hears them, and finds something true.

teach.h: EACH SIDE HOLDS A REAL PIECE.
teach.b: Quarrels are often like that: each side holds a real piece, a real hurt, a real fact, a real fear. The story cuts the other way too.

A judge who agrees with everyone has decided nothing; the men still have their quarrel. Some things do need a decision, and the tale is laughing at Nasruddin as well. So it isn't telling you never to choose.
It's asking you to notice how fast you choose, and what you miss when you do.
Listen long enough to say, honestly, you're right, about something, to each person. Then decide, if you have to.

how: Nasruddin's judge stories are told across Turkey, Iran and Central Asia, often to children and in classrooms, as a joke about snap judgments; in some tellings the objector is his wife, in others a clerk or a neighbor.

games.q: you're the judge. both men have spoken, and both sounded convincing. someone says: they can't both be right! what do you say?
o: you're right, and I'll pick one now.
games.why: Nasruddin thinks it over and agrees with her too. it's a joke first, and it catches how fast we pick a winner.

practice: Bring to mind a disagreement you're close to, yours or someone else's, and let each person speak in your head. Find one thing each of them is right about; if you're one of the two, find what the other person is right about.
Don't decide who wins: hold both, the way Nasruddin does, and breathe.

wordCard.voice: qadi, the Arabic word for judge. Nasruddin held that role, finding something true in each person who speaks, even the one who says they can't both be right.

orig.note: Arabic, qadi: a judge. In Turkish it became kadı, the title Nasruddin holds in these tales.

carryVoice: Your line: you are also right. The joke is on the judge, too. Day thirty-nine, done.
